text:
The sacked boss of the Pride in London LGBTQ+ parade has been given a suspended prison sentence for his “flagrant” contempt of court when accessing the organisation’s records in breach of a judicial order.
Christopher Joell-Deshields, who was suspended as chief executive in summer 2025 and sacked in April, failed to give up access to Pride’s IT systems as ordered by the high court and instead “harvested” documents for his own use.
Between 50 and 60 internal documents were downloaded in September last year and used by Joell-Deshields to establish a rival LGBTQ+ event and to make a 208-page employment tribunal claim against Pride in London, in which he is claiming wrongful dismissal and discrimination.
London’s annual Pride parade is the largest LGBTQ+ event in the UK and attracts about 30,000 participants. It is funded by sponsors and a £125,000-a-year grant from the mayor of London.
Mr Justice Cotter said Joell-Deshields’ actions had been a “serious, wilful, flagrant flouting” of the high court. The judge said the defendant had avoided immediate imprisonment owing to his poor mental health and role as sole carer to his 15-year-old twin daughters.
Joell-Deshields, who was paid £87,500 a year as chief executive of London LGBT Community Pride, the body that trades as Pride in London, claimed in his witness statement to be “exhausted, overwhelmed and broken”. The judge said the court would not be as lenient if further evidence emerged of a breach of the courts order.
Joell-Deshields, who had been chief executive of Pride in London since 2021, was put under internal investigation in August 2025 and suspended the following month in response to whistleblowers’ claims of misconduct.
The allegations included bullying and the misuse of vouchers provided by an unnamed sponsor for volunteers at the Pride march, which he denies. Joell-Deshields was subsequently sacked.
In September, London LGBT Community Pride successfully applied to the high court for an injunction that would force Joell-Deshields to hand over company property and passwords for online accounts, including banks, Facebook and HM Revenue and Customs.
Joell-Deshields failed to comply with the order, under which he was also required to provide a statement confirming that he had given up or destroyed property belonging to the community interest company.
Rather than hand over the passwords and documents, Joell-Deshields used his access to Pride’s records to download documents, including privileged information he subsequently used in his employment claim.
Joell-Deshields claimed to the court that he had merely taken notes and that he could not recall downloading the information.
Cotter said this version of events was “unbelievable” and ruled that he had “harvested” the documents on 15 September last year, three days after being issued with a court order.
“I don’t accept that he does not recollect undertaking this exercise,” the judge said. “The court will not tolerate deliberate disobedience of such orders.”
Joell-Deshields, who it was claimed owned two houses in London, was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment for contempt in failing to hand over property and passwords and a concurrent jail sentence of four months for failing to submit his statement detailing the records he had held. The sentences are suspended for 18 months. He will also pay costs.
